summary: Letting a node choose a forwarding path other than the shortest one benefits many network functions, yet earlier source-based routing mechanisms saw little adoption. This informational RFC gives the SPRING problem statement and requirements, where source means where the explicit route is imposed.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers usually choose a shortest path, but operators sometimes need a packet to take another route. This RFC explains the problems and requirements behind source packet routing.

subtitle: Why operators need to impose packet paths and what the SPRING architecture must support.

tldr.problem: Operators need to send traffic along paths other than normal shortest paths for functions such as protection and traffic engineering.
tldr.mechanism: SPRING places explicit routing policy in the packet header, allowing the source of the route to choose paths without per-hop signaling or policy state at intermediate routers.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC describes unicast use cases and requirements. Multicast use cases are outside its scope.

facts.label: Traffic scope
facts.value: Unicast; multicast is out of scope

today: RFC 7855 is an Informational problem statement and requirements document published in May 2016. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Source Routing Is Useful
sections.content:
Allowing a node to specify a unicast forwarding path can support network virtualization, protection, programmability, operations and maintenance, load balancing, and traffic engineering. Earlier source-routing mechanisms existed but had not seen widespread adoption except for MPLS traffic engineering.

In this RFC, the source is the point where an explicit route is imposed. It may be the operator's network ingress, not the original packet sender. The architecture is intended to allow incremental deployment without a network-wide upgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can choose a route for a packet instead of relying only on the normal shortest path. The route may be added at the network entrance, even if the packet started elsewhere.

sections.title: Tunneling, Recovery, and Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
The RFC discusses IGP-based MPLS tunnels for services such as VPNs, fast reroute using precomputed backup paths, and traffic engineering. It also requires interoperability between SPRING-capable and non-SPRING nodes.

Traffic engineering may use loose routes that specify key hops or strict routes that specify every hop. Requirements include ECMP awareness, optional bandwidth admission control, disjoint paths in dual-plane networks, egress peer engineering, and load sharing over non-parallel links.
sections.plainLanguage: The use cases include sending VPN traffic across a chosen path, switching to a backup after a failure, and steering selected traffic. Operators may specify only key hops or the full path.

sections.title: Packet Policy and Data Planes
sections.content:
The architecture MUST put policy state in the packet header rather than in intermediate nodes. It MUST allow selective deployment and interoperability with nodes that do not support SPRING.

The RFC says the design SHOULD use the existing MPLS data plane without modification and SHOULD use IPv6 with a new routing header. It also says the architecture should be general enough for different data planes.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet carries the route instructions, so middle routers do not need policy state for each service. The architecture is intended to work with existing MPLS and IPv6 networks.

sections.title: Fast Recovery and Network State
sections.content:
For fast reroute, the architecture MUST support backup paths on any topology and allow their precomputation and setup without extra signaling beyond regular IGP or BGP protocols. It must support shared-risk constraints, node and link protection, and micro-loop avoidance.

For traffic engineering, the RFC calls for limiting per-service state and signaling on midpoint and tail-end routers, supporting ECMP-aware paths, and keeping the policy resilient to failure of a specific core node.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup route should be ready without adding a separate signaling exchange through the network. The routing policy should not depend on one core router remaining available.

sections.title: Trust Boundaries and Security
sections.content:
Because packets carry source-routing information, an attacker who changes the header may change the path and cause an outage. The architecture MUST define trust boundaries so source-routing information is usable only inside the trusted domain and is not exposed outside it.

Filtering is required at domain boundaries in the forwarding plane. The RFC says the architecture must evaluate authentication and validation mechanisms for source-routing information, and each data-plane and control-plane document must address its security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted nodes should impose routes, and route instructions must not leak outside the trusted network. Boundary routers need to filter this information.

items.text: Carry services between provider edge routers.

items.title: Fast reroute

items.title: Traffic engineering
items.text: Steer traffic to meet network requirements.

items.title: Interoperability
items.text: Coexist with nodes that do not support SPRING.
